title: Michael Thorbjornsen keeps PGA’s youth movement rolling, rallies to win Rocket Classic
content:
The youth wave continues.

Trailing a leaderboard full of major winners, top-tier stars and players four shots ahead, 24-year-old Michael Thorbjornsen shot a bogey-free 63 to break through at the Rocket Classic for his first career PGA Tour win. It comes just a week after rookie phenom Jackson Koivun won in his third professional start.

For Thorbjornsen, it took five birdies on the back nine to catapult him past Xander Schauffele, Rasmus Hojgaard and Davis Riley and prove he has staying power. The young talent hit a 26-foot birdie on 18 to seal it for a two-shot win.

What tells you more about Thorbjornsen, though, is the difference in how he handled pressure.

He might owe a thank you to Ludvig Åberg. If it weren’t for Åberg putting two balls on the back nine in the water to collapse at the Players Championship in March, it may have been Thorbjornsen who was the larger conversation that Sunday. Playing in the final group together, two 20-something former prized amateurs contending for the biggest tournament on the PGA Tour, Thorbjornsen made a mess of his own. He scored an 8 on the fourth hole to drop from T2 to ultimately T22.

Yet he never viewed that as some nervous moment. The cool, calm Stanford product said he actually was surprised how comfortable he felt. No excuses, he said. Just bad shots.

“I feel like that wasn’t because of nerves or anything,” he said two weeks later in Houston. “It was just I need to get better at my wedges.”

This win makes it two weeks in a row a recent PGA Tour University graduate earned their first win, as just last week the Auburn prodigy Koivun won the 3M Open in his third professional start.

The last time two 24-or-younger Americans got their first career PGA Tour wins in consecutive weeks was in 2017. Those two were Xander Schauffele and Bryson DeChambeau.

Thorbjornsen wasn’t quite the historic prodigy Åberg or Koivun were. He didn’t win on tour as an amateur like Nick Dunlap or build a hype train like Luke Clanton. But he too earned the PGA Tour University designation, giving him an immediate Tour card when he turned pro in 2024. But while Clanton and Dunlap have struggled mightily in their rookie campaigns, Thorbjornsen proved himself quickly but quietly. He earned eight top 10s in his first 16 months as a pro.

Then, in 2026, he started truly contending in big events. He put himself at the top of the leaderboard at the Waste Management Phoenix Open and the aforementioned Players while dramatically improving his short game.

Yet that first win didn’t come as the favorite or even a top contender. It came from four shots back with seven names above him on the leaderboard. It came as Thorbjornsen’s short game, once an issue, holed out from the rough on 12 and produced a tap-in birdie on 14. And it came while leading the field in iron play, gaining 3.53 shots in approach in the final round.

With the win, Thorbjornsen jumps from 69th to 38th in the FedEx Cup standings, confirming a place in the tour playoffs and in a good position to make the top 50, earning himself exemptions into all signature events next year.

Most of all, though, he proved something far more valuable in this world. He proved he’s a winner.
